title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
claim: Sparse autoencoders recover ground-truth latent modes better than classical sparse baselines as embedding dimension grows, with recovery saturating near the true mode count.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared x-axis, vertical line marks ground-truth count
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the x-axis, embedding dimension m, running 16 to 128 on a log-like scale. The left panel shows median per-feature Pearson correlation with the best-matching ground-truth mode. The center panel shows mean cosine similarity between codes and ground-truth weights. The right panel shows the fraction of modes recovered at cosine ≥ 0.7. Three methods are drawn in bold with shaded std bands: SAE-SFD in light blue, SAE in dark blue, and SAE (merged) as a dashed red line with square markers. Classical baselines (Random, PCA, ICA, K-Means, NMF, and an Oracle ceiling) are thin grey lines. A faint vertical line marks m=75, the true mode count. The eye goes first to the bold blue and red curves rising toward the top right. The legend sits in the center panel.
caption: Mode recovery vs. embedding dimension m (mean ± 1 std over 5 random projections). Left: median per-feature Pearson r with best-matching ground-truth mode. Center: mean per-user cosine similarity between projected codes and ground-truth weight vector. Right: fraction of modes recovered at decoder–centroid cosine similarity ≥0.7. The vertical line marks m = 75, the ground-truth mode count.
abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines. We then apply our methods to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.
